title: Cleaning Up Is Part of the Transformation
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: Drawing on years in vehicle-development project leadership, Uwe Mierisch dissects an organization's habit of running projects into crisis and then pulling off heroic, last-minute rescues that get celebrated every time the cycle repeats. He argues the uncomfortable insight is that the organization already had the capability for focus, collaboration, and compromise all along, but pressure was the only trigger reliable enough to surface it, meaning the real task is moving that performance to the front of a project as a daily habit rather than an emergency reflex. He places responsibility for the pattern squarely on leadership, since organizations repeat whatever gets rewarded, and rescues get rewarded while quiet, on-track delivery in the middle of a project does not. The piece's sharpest turn addresses AI and technological transformation as a newly available excuse for skipping this unglamorous cleanup work, arguing that laying new technology over a broken process does not fix the process but industrializes its dysfunction, making it come back faster and harder to control. He closes by rejecting the idea that transformation and process cleanup are alternatives, insisting an organization has to do both simultaneously or won't survive either one.
points: Reframes the heroic last-minute project rescue not as a success story but as evidence the organization already had the capability for focus and compromise all along - it simply required crisis-level pressure to surface it.

Names the specific leadership failure precisely: organizations reward the rescue, not the quiet, on-track middle of a project, so the celebrated behavior is the one that guarantees the pattern repeats.

Identifies AI and technological transformation as a newly 'respectable' excuse to skip unglamorous process repair, arguing the logic ('why fix what's about to be obsolete') sounds forward-looking while actually avoiding the harder work.

Makes the mechanism of harm explicit: new technology laid over a broken process doesn't repair it, it industrializes the dysfunction, so whatever was disorganized before returns faster, at greater scale, and harder to control.

Rejects the false choice between transformation and process cleanup outright, arguing organizations attempting both at once with the same people must treat them as one combined obligation, not sequential or competing priorities.
quotes: Every time there was relief. Every time a huge pride. People were recognized as heroes, and treated like heroes. We had done it again. But the celebration was short, because the next crisis was already there.
a rescue that works every time is only a rescue until the one time it does not. A vehicle manufacturer without a product survives a few weeks. Then it is over

The organization could do it. The capability was there, all of it, and it was impressive. It simply would not come out until the crisis had arrived. Pressure was the trigger, and nothing else worked as reliably.

An organization repeats what it sees rewarded, and what gets rewarded is usually the rescue. A team that is quietly on track in the middle of a project deserves the recognition that goes to the heroes at the end.
If everything is going to be different anyway, why repair a process that will be obsolete in a few years? Why insist on human performance when the technology is going to take it over regardless?
a new technology laid on top of a broken process does not repair the process. It industrializes it. Whatever was disorganized before comes back faster, at scale, and harder to control
Cleaning up is not the sober alternative to transforming, and transforming is not permission to skip the cleaning up. We have to do both. Either one on its own will not be enough to still be here.
